faq.a: Low iodine reduces hormone synthesis, raising TSH, which stimulates thyroid growth before hormone levels fall enough to cause symptoms.
faq.q: Why does goitre appear before hypothyroid symptoms?

faq.a: Yes, especially in people with autonomous nodules; excess iodine can trigger the Jod‑Basedow phenomenon.
An acute, self‑limiting inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis after a large iodine load; the gland normally escapes after 24‑48 h.

exam: A 7‑year‑old from a rural village presents with a diffuse goitre and mild developmental delay – what is the most likely diagnosis and first public‑health intervention? — Iodine deficiency; start iodised oil and promote iodised salt.

A patient on potassium iodide for a CT scan develops atrial fibrillation – which mechanism explains this and what immediate drug should be given? — Iodine‑induced thyrotoxicosis (Jod‑Basedow); give a β‑blocker.

Explain why serum TSH may be normal in early iodine deficiency despite a palpable goitre. — TSH rises but may still be within reference range due to compensatory up‑regulation; goitre reflects chronic TSH stimulation.

How does the Wolff‑Chaikoff effect protect the thyroid, and why does it not cause permanent hypothyroidism? — Acute iodine excess blocks organification; the gland ‘escapes’ by down‑regulating NIS after 24‑48 h.

A pregnant woman in a coastal area has a borderline low urinary iodine – what counseling should you give? — Advise use of iodised salt, prenatal vitamins with iodine, and avoid excess goitrogenic foods.

Differentiate between toxic multinodular goitre and iodine‑deficiency goitre on clinical grounds. — Toxic: nodular, suppressed TSH, symptoms of hyperthyroidism; Deficiency: diffuse, elevated TSH, hypothyroid features.

What laboratory test would you order if thyroid scintigraphy is unavailable, and how would you interpret it? — Measure serum TSH and free T4; low TSH with high T4 suggests hyperthyroidism, high TSH with low T4 suggests hypothyroidism.
In a patient with suspected iodine excess but no lab, what bedside clue helps you suspect thyrotoxicosis? — New‑onset tachycardia, tremor, heat intolerance, and recent iodine‑containing medication.
ai.title: Iodine Metabolism and Thyroid Function
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Iodine is taken up by the thyroid, organified, and incorporated into thyroid hormones. Understanding this pathway helps diagnose and manage disorders like goitre, hypothyroidism, and iodine deficiency, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Absorption: 90% in duodenum/jejunum
Transport: bound to albumin, iodide
Uptake: NIS, stimulated by TSH
Organification: thyroid peroxidase (TPO)
Hormone release: T3 (5%) and T4 (95%)
sections.p: Iodine is an essential trace element. After oral intake it is absorbed in the small intestine, circulates bound to plasma proteins, and is actively taken up by the thyroid via the sodium‑iodide symporter (NIS). Inside the gland iodine is oxidised, attached to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin, and coupled to form T3 and T4, which are released into the bloodstream.

b: Iodine deficiency → low T3/T4 → ↑TSH → goitre
Iodine excess → Wolff‑Chaikoff effect → transient ↓ hormone synthesis
Auto‑immune thyroiditis can impair organification despite adequate iodine
sections.p: The rate‑limiting step is iodine uptake; therefore NIS function and dietary iodine determine hormone output. Iodine excess or deficiency shifts the feedback loop, altering TSH and causing goitre or thyroid dysfunction.

b: Goitre: palpable thyroid enlargement, may cause dysphagia
Hypothyroidism: fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain
Hyperthyroidism from iodine load: atrial fibrillation, tremor
sections.p: In East Africa iodine deficiency remains common, especially in inland regions without iodised salt. Presentations include diffuse goitre, cretinism in children, and hypothyroid symptoms in adults. Iodine excess from supplements or contrast can precipitate thyroiditis.

t.b: Is thyroid output suppressed or stimulated? ↑TSH suggests deficiency or primary hypothyroidism; ↓TSH suggests excess iodine or hyperthyroidism
Confirms hormone status; low in deficiency, high in iodine‑induced thyrotoxicosis
Assesses recent iodine intake; <100 µg/L indicates deficiency, >300 µg/L suggests excess. If lab unavailable, use dietary history.

b: Explain why goitre can be present with normal TSH in early deficiency
Describe the acute Wolff‑Chaikoff effect and its escape phenomenon
Identify the most cost‑effective prevention: universal salt iodisation
sections.p: Examiners love to test the feedback loop, the Wolff‑Chaikoff effect, and public‑health measures.

b: Assuming a palpable goitre always means malignancy
Neglecting dietary history in low‑resource settings
Ordering radioactive iodine uptake when scintigraphy is unavailable
sections.p: Students often confuse iodine deficiency with autoimmune thyroid disease or assume that all goitres need surgery.

b: Excess: stop iodine source, give β‑blocker for symptomatic thyrotoxicosis, consider glucocorticoids if severe
Hypothyroidism: levothyroxine after repletion, monitor TSH in 6‑8 weeks
sections.p: Treat the underlying iodine imbalance first, then address hormone levels and complications.

b: Autoimmune thyroiditis – antibodies present, often euthyroid
Toxic multinodular goitre – nodules, suppressed TSH
Thyroid carcinoma – hard, irregular mass, may have cervical lymphadenopathy
sections.p: Differential diagnoses for goitre and thyroid dysfunction.

b: Serum TSH may be normal in early iodine deficiency (compensated phase)
Urinary iodine can be falsely low if sample is dilute; correct for creatinine if possible

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden neck swelling with respiratory distress
Severe tachyarrhythmia or heart failure in a patient with recent iodine load
Acute encephalopathy in a child with suspected severe iodine deficiency
